--- title: "Discrete Probability Distributions" output: pdf_document: number_sections: yes html_document: default editor_options: chunk_output_type: console editor: markdown: wrap: sentence --- ## Random Variables A **random variable** is a numeric variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a random experiment. Random variables are denoted with capital letters ($X$, $Y$) and their specific realized values with lowercase letters ($x$, $y$). - A **discrete random variable** takes a countable number of values (finite or countably infinite), e.g., number of ER visits in a month. - A **continuous random variable** takes any value within an interval (covered in Section 8), e.g., blood pressure. ## Probability Mass Function (PMF) For a discrete random variable $X$, the **probability mass function (PMF)**, $P(X=x)$, gives the probability that $X$ takes on each specific value $x$. A valid PMF must satisfy: 1. $0 \le P(X=x) \le 1$ for every $x$ 2. $\sum_{\text{all } x} P(X=x) = 1$ The **cumulative distribution function (CDF)** is $F(x) = P(X \le x) = \sum_{k\le x} P(X=k)$. ## Expected Value The **expected value** (mean) of a discrete random variable is the long-run average value, weighted by probability: $$E(X) = \mu = \sum_{\text{all } x} x\, P(X=x)$$ ## Variance $$Var(X) = \sigma^2 = \sum_{\text{all }x}(x-\mu)^2 P(X=x) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2$$ **Worked example:** A community health worker screens patients. let $X$ = number of positive screens out of the first 3 patients tested, with PMF: $P(0)=0.20$ $P(1)=0.35$ $P(2)=0.30$ $P(3)=0.15$ **Step 1:** Verify PMF sums to 1: $0.20+0.35+0.30+0.15=1.00$ **Step 2:** $E(X) = 0(0.20)+1(0.35)+2(0.30)+3(0.15) = 0+0.35+0.60+0.45=1.40$ **Step 3:**$E(X^2) = 0^2(0.20)+1^2(0.35)+2^2(0.30)+3^2(0.15)=0+0.35+1.20+1.35=2.90$ **Step 4:** $Var(X) = 2.90-1.40^2=2.90-1.96=0.94$ $SD(X)=\sqrt{0.94}=0.97$. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Bernoulli Distribution ### Definition Models a **single trial** with exactly two possible outcomes: "success" (1) or "failure" (0). ### PMF $$P(X=x) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x \in \{0,1\}$$ ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $p$ = probability of success | |-----------|------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = p$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = p(1-p)$ | **Derivation of mean:** $E(X) = 0\cdot(1-p) + 1\cdot p = p$ **Derivation of variance:** $E(X^2) = 0^2(1-p)+1^2(p) = p$ $Var(X) = E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2 = p-p^2=p(1-p)$. ### Shape & Assumptions - Two-point distribution - Shape depends entirely on $p$. - Assumes a single trial with a fixed success probability. ### Applications / Public Health Example Whether a single patient tests positive for a disease ($p$ = prevalence); whether a single newborn is preterm; the building block for the Binomial distribution. ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- 0.3 x <- c(0, 1) prob <- dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = p) ggplot(data.frame(x = factor(x), prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + labs(title = "Bernoulli(p = 0.3)", x = "X", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/bernoulli-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ### Manual Calculation If prevalence of a risk factor 30% ($p = 0.30$). $P(X=1) = 0.30$ $P(X=0)=0.70$ Mean $=0.30$ Variance $=0.30(0.70)=0.21$ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Binomial Distribution ### Definition Models the number of **successes in** $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability of success $p$. ### PMF $$P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}, \quad x=0,1,\ldots,n$$ where $\binom{n}{x} = \dfrac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}$. ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $n$ = number of trials, $p$ = probability of success | |-----------|------------------------------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = np$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = np(1-p)$ | ### Shape - Symmetric when $p=0.5$ - Right-skewed when $p<0.5$ and left-skewed when $p>0.5$ - Approaches a Normal shape as $n$ grows (for fixed $p$ not too close to 0 or 1). It is a consequence of the Central Limit Theorem. ### Assumptions 1. Fixed number of trials $n$. 2. Each trial has only two outcomes. 3. Constant probability of success $p$ across trials. 4. Trials are independent. ### Applications / Public Health Example Number of patients who respond to treatment out of $n$ treated; number of children vaccinated out of $n$ eligible; number of surgical-site infections out of $n$ surgeries. ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 20; p <- 0.3 x <- 0:n prob <- dbinom(x, size = n, prob = p) ggplot(data.frame(x, prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "darkorange") + labs(title = "Binomial(n = 20, p = 0.3)", x = "Number of successes", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/binomial-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ### Worked Example (Manual Calculation) In a clinic, 30% of screened patients ($p=0.3$) are found to have elevated cholesterol. Out of $n=5$ patients screened today, what is the probability exactly 2 have elevated cholesterol? **Step 1:** Identify $n=5$, $x=2$, $p=0.3$ **Step 2:** Compute the binomial coefficient: $\binom{5}{2} = \dfrac{5!}{2!3!} = \dfrac{120}{2\times 6}=10$ **Step 3:** Compute $p^x = 0.3^2 = 0.09$ and $(1-p)^{n-x} = 0.7^3=0.343$. **Step 4:** Multiply: $$P(X=2) = 10 \times 0.09 \times 0.343 = 0.3087 \approx 30.9\%$$ **Verification in R:** `dbinom(2, size = 5, prob = 0.3)` returns 0.3087. Mean $= np = 5(0.3) = 1.5$ patients Variance $= np(1-p)=5(0.3)(0.7)=1.05$ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Geometric Distribution ### Definition Models the **number of trials needed to obtain the first success** in a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials. ### PMF $$P(X=x) = (1-p)^{x-1}p, \quad x=1,2,3,\ldots$$ (Convention: $X$ counts the trial *on which* the first success occurs. An alternative parameterization counts the number of *failures before* the first success, $Y=X-1$.) ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $p$ = probability of success per trial | |-----------|----------------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = \dfrac{1}{p}$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = \dfrac{1-p}{p^2}$ | ### Shape & Assumptions - Always right-skewed - Highest probability at $x=1$, decreasing geometrically thereafter. - Assumes independent trials with constant $p$, continuing until the first success (a "waiting time" distribution). ### Applications / Public Health Example - Number of couples' pregnancy attempts (cycles) until conception - Number of blood donors screened until finding one with a specific rare blood type - Number of contact-tracing attempts until successfully reaching a contact. ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- 0.25 x <- 1:15 prob <- dgeom(x - 1, prob = p) # R's dgeom counts failures before success ggplot(data.frame(x, prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "seagreen") + labs(title = "Geometric(p = 0.25), X = trial of first success", x = "Trial number of first success", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/geometric-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ::: callout-tip R's `dgeom(k, prob)` defines $k$ as the number of **failures before** the first success, so to match the "trial number" parameterization above, use `dgeom(x - 1, prob)`. ::: ### Worked Example (Manual Calculation) If 25% of blood donors ($p=0.25$) have blood type O-negative, what is the probability that the **4th** donor screened is the first one with O-negative blood? **Step 1:** $x=4$, $p=0.25$, so $1-p=0.75$ **Step 2:** Apply the PMF\ $$P(X=4) = (0.75)^{3}(0.25) = 0.4219\times0.25 = 0.1055 \approx 10.6\%$$ **Mean** $= 1/0.25 = 4$ donors (on average, expect to screen 4 donors to find one O-negative). **Variance** $= (1-0.25)/0.25^2 = 0.75/0.0625=12$. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Negative Binomial Distribution ### Definition Generalizes the Geometric distribution: models the **number of trials needed to achieve the** $r$-th success. ### PMF $$P(X=x) = \binom{x-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^{x-r}, \quad x=r,r+1,r+2,\ldots$$ ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $r$ = target number of successes, $p$ = probability of success per trial | |------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = \dfrac{r}{p}$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = \dfrac{r(1-p)}{p^2}$ | ### Shape & Assumptions - Right-skewed (less so as $r$ increases) - Same independence/constant-$p$ assumptions as the Geometric distribution (which is the special case $r=1$). - Also widely used (in its alternative "count" parameterization) to model **overdispersed count data**, count data whose variance exceeds its mean, which the Poisson distribution cannot accommodate. ### Applications / Public Health Example - Number of patients that must be screened to identify $r=3$ cases of a rare disease for a case series. - Modeling overdispersed disease counts (e.g., hospital readmission counts) where a Poisson model underestimates variability. ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} r <- 3; p <- 0.25 x <- r:30 prob <- dnbinom(x - r, size = r, prob = p) # R counts failures before r-th success ggplot(data.frame(x, prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "purple") + labs(title = "Negative Binomial(r = 3, p = 0.25)", x = "Trial of 3rd success", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/negbinom-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ### Worked Example (Manual Calculation) Continuing the O-negative blood donor example ($p=0.25$): what is the probability that the **6th** donor screened is the one who provides the **3rd** O-negative unit found ($r=3$)? **Step 1:** $x=6$, $r=3$, $p=0.25$ **Step 2:** Binomial coefficient: $\binom{x-1}{r-1} = \binom{5}{2} = 10$ **Step 3:** $p^r = 0.25^3 = 0.015625$ $(1-p)^{x-r} = 0.75^3 = 0.421875$ **Step 4:** $$P(X=6) = 10\times 0.015625\times 0.421875 = 0.0659 \approx 6.6\%$$ Mean $= r/p = 3/0.25=12$ donors expected to find 3 O-negative units. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Hypergeometric Distribution ### Definition Models the number of successes in $n$ draws **without replacement** from a finite population of size $N$ containing $K$ successes, used when sampling is done **without replacement** from a small, finite population (in contrast to the Binomial, which assumes independence/replacement). ### PMF $$P(X=x) = \frac{\binom{K}{x}\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}}$$ ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $N$ = population size, $K$ = number of successes in population, $n$ = sample size | |--------------------------|----------------------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = n\dfrac{K}{N}$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = n\dfrac{K}{N}\cdot\dfrac{N-K}{N}\cdot\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}$ | The variance formula includes the **finite population correction factor**, $\dfrac{N-n}{N-1}$, which distinguishes it from the Binomial. ### Shape & Assumptions - Similar in shape to the Binomial for large $N$ relative to $n$ (in fact, the Hypergeometric converges to the Binomial as $N\to\infty$ with $K/N=p$ fixed). - Assumes sampling **without replacement** from a finite, known population. ### Applications / Public Health Example Selecting a sample of vials for quality control from a finite batch (as in Section 4's defective-vial example); selecting a committee/sample from a small finite roster of patients with known disease status; capture-recapture population size estimation. ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} N <- 50; K <- 10; n <- 8 x <- 0:min(n, K) prob <- dhyper(x, m = K, n = N - K, k = n) ggplot(data.frame(x, prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "firebrick") + labs(title = "Hypergeometric(N=50, K=10, n=8)", x = "Number of successes", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/hypergeom-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ### Worked Example (Manual Calculation) A batch of $N=50$ vaccine vials contains $K=10$ expired vials. A quality inspector randomly selects $n=5$ vials for testing (without replacement). What is the probability exactly $x=2$ are expired? **Step 1:** $\binom{K}{x} = \binom{10}{2} = 45$ **Step 2:** $\binom{N-K}{n-x} = \binom{40}{3} = 9880$ **Step 3:** $\binom{N}{n} = \binom{50}{5} = 2{,}118{,}760$ **Step 4:** $$P(X=2) = \frac{45\times9880}{2{,}118{,}760} = \frac{444{,}600}{2{,}118{,}760}=0.2099\approx21.0\%$$ Mean $= n(K/N) = 5(10/50)=1.0$ expired vial expected in the sample. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Poisson Distribution ### Definition Models the number of **rare, independent events occurring in a fixed interval** of time, space, or exposure, when events happen at a constant average rate $\lambda$. ### PMF $$P(X=x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}, \quad x=0,1,2,\ldots$$ ### Parameters, Mean, Variance | Parameter | $\lambda$ = mean (and rate) of events per interval | |-----------|----------------------------------------------------| | Mean | $E(X) = \lambda$ | | Variance | $Var(X) = \lambda$ | The Poisson is unique in that its **mean equals its variance**, an assumption that is often violated in real disease-count data (overdispersion), motivating the use of the Negative Binomial as an alternative. ### Shape & Assumptions - Right-skewed for small $\lambda$, approaching a symmetric, Normal-like shape as $\lambda$ increases. - Assumes: - events occur independently, - at a constant average rate, - two events cannot occur at exactly the same instant, - the number of events in non-overlapping intervals is independent. ### Applications / Public Health Example Number of new cases of a rare disease reported per month in a district; number of hospital-acquired infections per 1000 patient-days; number of deaths from a rare adverse drug reaction; number of disease outbreaks per year in a region. The Poisson also arises as the limiting distribution of the Binomial when $n$ is large, $p$ is small, and $np=\lambda$ is moderate (the "law of rare events"). ### R Code and Graph ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lambda <- 4 x <- 0:15 prob <- dpois(x, lambda = lambda) ggplot(data.frame(x, prob), aes(x, prob)) + geom_col(fill = "slateblue") + labs(title = "Poisson(lambda = 4)", x = "Number of events", y = "P(X = x)") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_discrete_probability_distributions_files/figure-pdf/poisson-1.pdf){fig-align='center' fig-pos='H' width=85%} ::: ::: ### Worked Example (Manual Calculation) A district reports an average of $\lambda=4$ cases of a rare disease per month. What is the probability that exactly 6 cases are reported next month? **Step 1:** $\lambda=4$, $x=6$ **Step 2:** $e^{-\lambda} = e^{-4} = 0.01832$ **Step 3:** $\lambda^x = 4^6=4096$ **Step 4:** $x! = 6! = 720$ **Step 5:** $$P(X=6) = \frac{0.01832\times4096}{720} = \frac{75.03}{720}=0.1042\approx10.4\%$$ **Verification in R:** `dpois(6, lambda = 4)` returns 0.1042. **Probability of zero cases:** $P(X=0) = e^{-4}(4^0)/0! = e^{-4} = 0.0183$. It means 1.8% chance of no cases reported at all next month. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Comparison Table — Discrete Distributions | Distribution | Models | Parameters | Mean | Variance | Trials fixed? | Sampling | |-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------| | Bernoulli | Single success/failure | $p$ | $p$ | $p(1-p)$ | 1 trial | | | Binomial | \# successes in $n$ trials | $n,p$ | $np$ | $np(1-p)$ | Yes | With replacement / independent | | Geometric | \# trials to 1st success | $p$ | $1/p$ | $(1-p)/p^2$ | No (random) | With replacement / independent | | Negative Binomial | \# trials to $r$-th success | $r,p$ | $r/p$ | $r(1-p)/p^2$ | No (random) | With replacement / independent | | Hypergeometric | \# successes in $n$ draws, finite pop. | $N,K,n$ | $nK/N$ | $n\frac{K}{N}\frac{N-K}{N}\frac{N-n}{N-1}$ | Yes | **Without** replacement | | Poisson | \# events in fixed interval | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ | N/A (rate-based) | | ## Decision Guide: Which Distribution Should I Use? ```{mermaid} flowchart TD Q1{"Are you counting events
per unit time/space
(no fixed 'n')?"} -->|Yes| Poisson["Use Poisson"] Q1 -->|No, fixed number of trials/draws| Q2{"Sampling with or without
replacement from a
finite, small population?"} Q2 -->|Without replacement, finite pop.| Hyper["Use Hypergeometric"] Q2 -->|With replacement / independent trials, or infinite population| Q3{"Are you counting
successes in n fixed trials,
or waiting for success(es)?"} Q3 -->|"Counting successes in fixed n"| Q4{"n = 1 trial?"} Q4 -->|Yes| Bern["Use Bernoulli"] Q4 -->|No, n > 1| Binom["Use Binomial"] Q3 -->|"Waiting for success(es)"| Q5{"Waiting for 1st success
or r-th success?"} Q5 -->|"1st success"| Geo["Use Geometric"] Q5 -->|"r-th success"| NB["Use Negative Binomial"] ``` ## Summary - A **random variable** maps outcomes of a random experiment to numbers; its **PMF** assigns probabilities to each possible value. - **Expected value** and **variance** summarize the center and spread of a discrete distribution. - **Bernoulli** (1 trial) generalizes to **Binomial** ($n$ trials); **Geometric** (wait for 1st success) generalizes to **Negative Binomial** (wait for $r$-th success). - **Hypergeometric** is the without-replacement analogue of the Binomial for finite populations. - **Poisson** models rare events over a fixed interval and is the limiting case of the Binomial as $n\to\infty$, $p\to0$, with $np=\lambda$ fixed. Next section will deal with the probability distribution of **continuous variables**.
